newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's Camet sees Feb inflation below 0.5 pct.
newsitem.headline: Peru's Camet sees Feb inflation below 0.5 pct.

text.p: Peru's Economy Minister Jorge Camet said February inflation is likely to be below 0.5 percent and that the government does not plan to alter its floating exchange-rate policy.
"There are indications it will be less than half of one percent. It looks like it will be below that," Camet told local radio Monday night when asked about February's consumer price index.
Speaking at the annual meeting of Peru's National Exporters Society, Camet said the government is not worried about a possible year-end outbreak of inflation.
"On the contrary," he said. "With February's inflation, we are going to have an average for the last months below 10 percent. We will have broken the barrier."
Peru's consumer prices rose 0.48 percent in January, compared with a 1.2 percent rise in January 1996 and 1.2 percent in December, government figures show.

Consumer prices rose 11.84 percent last year versus 10.23 percent inflation in 1995. The government estimates accumulated inflation will be nine percent this year and will drop to "the level of industrialized countries" by 2000.
Camet, meanwhile, said the government does not plan to alter its exchange rate policy.
"There will be no modifications in management of the exchange rate," he said. "Management of the exchange rate will continue the same, floating with some action by the Central Bank when necessary."
Peruvian officials have resisted pressure by exporters' to reduce the dollar-sol exchange rate to enable local exports to be more competitive.

Camet said exports have doubled since President Alberto Fujimori was re-elected to a second five-year term in 1995 due partly to rebuilt roads, lower port costs and earnings from exchange-rate parity.
"Security costs also have been reduced, many costs have been reduced," Camet said.
